strengths: Addresses an important and timely challenge in speech processing: bridging the modality reasoning gap where Speech LLMs significantly underperform on spoken inputs compared to text.

Proposes a well-motivated on-policy reinforcement learning framework (TARS) with an asymmetric reward design, effectively combining coarse layer-wise hidden-state alignment with semantic behavior alignment.
Introduces modality-specific normalization in GRPO, preventing speech samples from being unfairly penalized by the text baseline during advantage estimation.

Demonstrates consistent and significant improvements across two 7B-scale Speech LLMs (Qwen2.5-Omni and Phi-4-MM) on MMSU and OBQA, outperforming both cascaded ASR-LLM baselines and existing alignment methods.

Provides insightful analytical experiments, including layer-depth sensitivity analysis (revealing middle layers as the primary site of representational drift) and teacher-forcing representation alignment curves.
weaknesses: Evaluation is restricted to multiple-choice benchmarks (MMSU and OBQA); evaluating on open-ended generation, spoken mathematical reasoning (e.g., spoken GSM8K), or multi-turn spoken dialogue would provide stronger evidence of generality.

Lacks an analysis of reward sparsity dynamics: the alignment rewards fall back to zero if no text completion in the group is correct, which may occur frequently on harder reasoning queries during early training phases.

The computational cost and memory overhead incurred by caching hidden states across all layers and querying an external embedding model (Qwen3-Embedding) inside the RL training loop are not systematically benchmarked.
Experiments are limited to the 7B parameter scale and freeze the audio encoder and adapter, leaving the impact of joint end-to-end updates unexplored.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely challenge in speech-language processing: the modality reasoning gap between speech and text inputs in end-to-end Speech LLMs.

Proposes a well-motivated reinforcement learning framework (TARS) with an asymmetric reward design, effectively combining dense layer-wise representation alignment to counteract internal drift with external semantic behavior alignment.
The inclusion of modality-specific advantage normalization within GRPO is a thoughtful methodological adaptation that prevents text-conditioned completions from dominating advantage baselines.

Empirical evaluations across two different 7B foundation models demonstrate clear improvements over both supervised alignment methods (e.g., SALAD, DeSTA, KD) and standard post-training strategies (SFT, DPO, standard GRPO).
Provides insightful ablation studies and analytical experiments, including layer-group sensitivity and layer-wise representation drift analyses, which support the mechanistic claims of the paper.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to multiple-choice spoken QA benchmarks (MMSU and OBQA from VoiceBench); evaluating on open-ended reasoning tasks, mathematical reasoning, or multi-turn dialogue would substantially strengthen the generality of the findings.

Training relies entirely on synthetic speech generated via TTS engines (CosyVoice2, openaudio-s1-mini) from text QA datasets, which may not adequately reflect real-world acoustic variations, background noise, disfluencies, or spontaneous spoken conversational dynamics.

The representation alignment reward computes a single mean-pooled representation over the generated tokens across layers, which may be coarse when speech and text reasoning trajectories differ in length, reasoning steps, or phrasing.

The computational overhead introduced by caching layer-wise hidden states and querying an external embedding model for every completion during on-policy rollout is non-trivial, but training latency/FLOPs comparisons against baseline methods are not detailed.

strengths: The paper addresses a significant and timely challenge in speech large language models: the modality reasoning gap where models perform substantially worse on spoken reasoning tasks than on text.

The technical formulation is well-motivated: using on-policy reinforcement learning (GRPO) with an asymmetric reward design combining dense layer-wise hidden state alignment and external semantic behavior alignment, along with modality-specific advantage normalization to prevent negative advantage dominance.

The empirical evaluation is solid, demonstrating consistent improvements over relevant and competitive baselines (e.g., cascaded ASR+LLM, KD, SFT, DPO, and standard GRPO) across two different 7B backbones.

The analytical depth is commendable; layer-sensitivity experiments and layer-wise representation drift visualizations (Figure 3) convincingly illustrate where and how the proposed rewards mitigate trajectory drift.
weaknesses: The benchmark evaluation is somewhat narrow in scope, being restricted to two multiple-choice datasets from VoiceBench (MMSU and OBQA). Testing on open-ended reasoning, mathematical problem solving (e.g., spoken GSM8K), or real-world conversational/human audio would provide a stronger test of generality.

The training dataset relies entirely on TTS-synthesized speech (CosyVoice2 and openaudio-s1-mini). While synthetic data is standard practice, there is little discussion or evaluation on how the alignment transfers to natural speech exhibiting conversational disfluencies, varied acoustic conditions, or strong accents.

The representation alignment metric averages hidden states across all tokens in the generated chain (Equation 4). Because reasoning chains can vary significantly in length and syntactic structure between speech and text generations, simple mean-pooling may dilute token-level progression and reasoning dynamics.
One of the two backbone models evaluated (Phi-4-MM-7B) is an internal unreleased checkpoint, which partially hinders full community reproducibility.

strengths: Well-motivated approach tackling the 'modality reasoning gap' in Speech LLMs through an on-policy reinforcement learning framework (TARS) rather than rigid supervised mimicry or frozen-adapter tuning.

The asymmetric reward design paired with modality-specific advantage normalization is technically sound and directly solves the issue of speech completions receiving consistently negative advantages in GRPO.

Solid empirical evaluation across two distinct 7B foundation architectures (Qwen2.5-Omni and Phi-4-MM), demonstrating clear improvements over strong baselines including cross-modal distillation, SFT, DPO, and cascaded pipelines.

Thorough ablation and diagnostic analyses, including layer-wise representation tracking, layer depth sensitivity, training efficiency profiling, and transparent reporting on differences in behavior between models.
weaknesses: The primary reasoning benchmarks are limited to multiple-choice formats (MMSU and OBQA), which may not fully assess generative multi-step reasoning capabilities compared to open-ended math or complex logical problem-solving tasks.

The training dataset relies exclusively on synthesized speech (TTS via CosyVoice2 and openaudio-s1-mini), which may lack natural speech phenomena like disfluencies, filler words, accents, and diverse acoustic noise environments.

The representation alignment reward (R_rep) degrades performance on Qwen2.5-Omni compared to behavior reward alone (R_beh) or even standard GRPO, indicating that strict layer-wise hidden-state similarity may over-regularize well-aligned foundation models.

Mean-pooling all reasoning hidden states across entire token sequences in Equation (4) collapses temporal dynamics and step-by-step structure in the reasoning chain, which may overlook local reasoning misalignments.

strengths: Addresses a timely and well-defined problem: the modality reasoning gap where Speech LLMs underperform on speech inputs compared to text inputs.
The proposed TARS framework provides a well-motivated on-policy alternative to existing rigid off-policy knowledge distillation and frozen-backbone adapter methods.

The RL design incorporates thoughtful mechanics, including asymmetric rewards that let text trajectories guide speech trajectories, and modality-specific advantage normalization to prevent speech rollout advantages from being systematically suppressed.

Strong empirical improvements over relevant post-training baselines (SFT, DPO, standard GRPO, and cross-modal distillation) across multiple-choice reasoning benchmarks (MMSU and OBQA) on two 7B architectures.

Extensive analysis and ablation studies, including layer-wise representation alignment curves, layer sensitivity analyses, and candid discussion of the different behaviors observed between an internal SFT model (Phi-4-MM) and an already aligned model (Qwen2.5-Omni).
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is largely concentrated on multiple-choice spoken QA (MMSU and OBQA). Broader evaluation on multi-step mathematical/algorithmic speech benchmarks (e.g., spoken GSM8K/MATH or SoundMind evaluation suites) would provide stronger evidence of general reasoning improvements.

Training relies exclusively on TTS-synthesized speech (UnifiedQA via CosyVoice2 and openaudio-s1-mini). TTS speech lacks natural acoustic variations, spontaneous disfluencies, and background noise, which leaves open questions about how robustly the trajectory alignment handles noisy or real conversational audio.

Inconsistency of the representation reward across models: Table 3 shows that adding the layer-wise representation reward (R_rep) degrades performance on Qwen2.5-Omni compared to behavior reward alone (R_beh), showing that the full combined objective does not generalize uniformly across different base models.

The representation reward computes cosine similarity over mean-pooled hidden states across the entire reasoning trace (up to 1,024 tokens). Mean-pooling across such long sequences risks washing out fine-grained, step-by-step reasoning dynamics.
Phi-4-MM is an internal checkpoint, which limits direct reproducibility of that half of the primary experimental results, though Qwen2.5-Omni results mitigate this somewhat.

strengths: Addresses a timely, significant, and persistent challenge in multimodal speech processing: the modality reasoning gap between speech- and text-conditioned generation in Speech LLMs.

Proposes a well-motivated reinforcement learning framework (TARS) combining asymmetric dense rewards (layer-wise representation similarity and semantic behavior similarity) with modality-specific advantage normalization to prevent gradient starvation in speech rollouts.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across two distinct 7B composite Speech LLMs (Qwen2.5-Omni and Phi-4-MM), demonstrating substantial gains on MMSU and OBQA benchmarks, matching or exceeding text-level reasoning performance (MRR ~100%) and surpassing cascaded ASR+LLM baselines.

Thorough analytical investigations and ablations, including layer-wise sensitivity analyses, tracking of ASR WER to decouple acoustic recognition from reasoning gains, text capability preservation checks, and computational efficiency breakdowns.
weaknesses: Inconsistent reward component behavior across model backbones: on Qwen2.5-Omni, incorporating representation alignment (R_rep) degrades performance relative to standard GRPO and behavior-only reward (R_beh), suggesting sensitivity to pretraining stages that may complicate tuning for new models.

Heavy reliance on synthetic speech (TTS) for post-training data; while common, synthetic audio lacks spontaneous speech characteristics such as natural disfluencies, varied acoustics, and realistic conversational noise.

Evaluation benchmarks are predominantly multiple-choice QA formats (MMSU, OBQA); testing on complex open-ended mathematical or multi-step logic benchmarks (e.g., spoken GSM8K/MATH) would provide a more complete assessment of long-chain reasoning capabilities.
